passage.title: 護照的演變（The Evolution of the Passport）
passage.text:
The concept of a travel document, which shows that a person is under a ruler’s protection while in a foreign land, has probably existed ever since the first rulers and states arose. But the earliest21of an object we might recognize as a passport dates from about 450 B.C. The Hebrew Bible states that Nehemiah, an official serving King Artaxerxes of ancient Persia, asked permission to travel to Judah. The king agreed and gave Nehemiah a letter “to the governors of the province beyond the river,”22safe passage for him as he traveled through their lands.

Centuries later, in the23period, the Islamic Caliphate used a form of passport called the bara’a, which was simply a receipt for taxes paid. Only those who had settled their taxes24the right to journey from one region of the Caliphate to another, so the receipt worked much like a travel pass.

Europe in the Middle Ages, on the other hand, took a different approach. There, travel documents were issued by local25and generally contained a list of the towns and cities that the holder was allowed to enter or pass through. On the whole, no papers were needed to reach seaports, which were regarded as26trading points that anyone could enter. Traveling27from a seaport, however, did require documents.

King Henry V of England is credited with having invented the first true passport, as a way of helping his28prove who they were in foreign lands. These documents were first29in a 15th-century Act of Parliament, though the Act did not yet call them “passports”; that term came into use about a century later. Even so, passports did not become a30requirement for international travel until the First World War. Only then did the passport take the form we know today.

passage.title: 叉子上桌記（How the Fork Reached the Table）
passage.text:
Forks trace their origins back to the ancient Greeks, yet many centuries passed before they became the dining tools we know today. records.explanation: 空格夾在 a 和 of 中間，要填單數名詞，但名詞選項不只一個。scene 最容易吸走人：a scene of the class warfare 讀成「階級鬥爭的一幕」，餐飲業卻成了鬥爭的現場，和「誕生」接不上。【作答線索】第一句用 gave birth to 講餐廳的來歷，還說這個誕生 hardly in a civilized way；第二句用 In fact 補充它是從什麼裡面生出來的：階級鬥爭。鬥爭的目的是推翻貴族，不是開餐廳，餐廳是順帶產生的結果，所以填 byproduct（副產品）。【文內驗證】第三、四段寫出經過：貴族出逃，失業的廚師進城，一年內開出將近 50 家餐廳。【延伸的字詞搭配】an unintended byproduct（意料之外的副產品）。

passage.title: 餐廳的誕生（The Birth of the Restaurant）
passage.text:
France gave birth to the restaurant, though hardly in a civilized way. In fact, today’s restaurant business is a21of the class warfare that arose during the French Revolution.

Back in the Middle Ages, fine dining was a22reserved for noble families, who had grand kitchens and personal chefs of their own. Ordinary people, by contrast, could eat out only at dusty, shabby roadside inns, where strangers crowded around23buffets of lukewarm roasts and over-sauced beans. But sometime in the 1760s, the merchant class of Paris24a taste for healthy clear broths that were believed to be restorative—hence the word “restaurant.” By the 1780s, this new Parisian “healthy food” craze had led to a handful of reputable dining halls, where customers could sit at their own tables and choose from a wide range of dishes.

Ironically, these dining halls grew popular at a time when most of the French population could not25bread. Decades of26winters and oppressive taxation had taken their toll on kitchen tables, and by 1789 the starving masses could no longer be controlled. Looting and riots broke out across Paris,27in the French Revolution.

Rich nobles fled to the countryside, leaving behind their highly skilled chefs and the fine wines stored in their cellars. Suddenly out of work, these cooks found their way to the city’s eateries, and within a year nearly 5028restaurants had popped up in Paris.

The restaurant business truly came into its own in the early 1800s, after General Napoleon seized control of the country. He granted “freedom of pleasure” to every citizen, reasoning that people absorbed in champagne and fine food would hardly conspire against him. The number of restaurants began to29sharply. By 1814, a popular travel guide listed about three thousand of them. Paris had become the center of a new restaurant30, and to some degree it remains so today.

records.explanation: usher 學生如果見過，記的是名詞「帶位員」；看到 ushering 不知道它能當動詞，就把它跳過。【一字多義】帶位員做的事是「領人進去」，所以動詞 usher 是「引導」，如 usher the guests into the hall（領客人進大廳）。把「領進門」用在事件上，usher in 就是「揭開……的序幕、迎來」：搶劫和暴動把法國大革命領了進來，也就是說，暴動是大革命的開端。【句構線索】逗號前已經是完整的句子，又沒有連接詞，逗號後只能用分詞；ushering 用主動的 V-ing，因為「揭開序幕」的是前面的搶劫和暴動。【延伸的字詞搭配】usher in a new era（開啟新時代）、usher in the New Year（迎接新年）。

records.explanation: 只看本句 nearly 50 ___ restaurants had popped up，好像什麼形容詞都放得進去，mediocre 最容易吸走人。關鍵在這些餐廳是誰開的，答案要往前一句找。【作答線索】前一句說貴族逃走，留下 highly skilled chefs（技術高超的廚師）和 fine wines（好酒）；本句前半說這些廚師進了城裡的餐館。一流的廚師帶著服侍貴族的手藝進城，開出來的是高級餐廳，所以填 elegant。【文內驗證】第五段的 champagne and fine food（香檳和美食）也是同一個方向，說的都是講究的飲食。【延伸的字詞搭配】an elegant restaurant／hotel（高級餐廳／氣派的飯店）。

records.explanation: rise 學生常在 a rise in prices（物價上漲）這類片語裡看到，當成名詞，就不往 began to 後面放；began to 後面要原形動詞，原形的選項又有 afford 和 rise 兩個。afford 是及物動詞，後面要接買得起的東西，這裡只有副詞 sharply，接不上。【怎麼判斷】主詞 The number of restaurants 要的是表示多少的動詞，number 搭配 rise、grow、increase、drop；sharply 說明變化很大，began to rise sharply 就是「開始急劇增加」。rise 同一個字形可以是名詞、也可以是動詞，要先讀懂句子才分得出來。【文內驗證】下一句說 1814 年的旅遊指南列了大約三千家餐廳，比第四段的將近 50 家多了好幾十倍。【延伸的字詞搭配】a sharp rise in sales（銷售額急劇增加）。

records.explanation: scene 學生記的是「場景、現場」，a new restaurant scene 翻成「新的餐廳場景」覺得不通，就不敢選。scene 另一個常用的意思是某個領域的整體活動和相關的人，也就是「……圈、……界」，如 the music scene（樂壇）、the art scene（藝術圈）。【怎麼判斷】a new restaurant ___ 前有冠詞和形容詞，restaurant 當修飾語，空格要單數名詞；privilege、byproduct 文法上也進得去，但「新的餐廳特權」「新的餐廳副產品」說不出意思。【文內驗證】前一句才說三千家餐廳列在旅遊指南上，巴黎成了整個餐飲圈的中心，句尾再補一句：在某種程度上，巴黎到今天仍然是這個圈子的中心。【延伸的字詞搭配】the local food scene（當地美食圈）。

passage.title: 腦中神曲（Earworms）
passage.text:
Music has a tendency to get stuck in our heads. Every so often, a tune21on our thoughts without warning. Once inside, it plays, and replays, in a never-ending22that may last anywhere from a few minutes to several hours. Scientists who study this curious phenomenon have given it a range of names—stuck-song syndrome, cognitive itch, and, most commonly, “earworm.” With each repetition, the melody grows more deeply23in the mind, so the brain keeps playing it even when the ears hear nothing at all.

Earworms seldom consist of entire songs. Instead, they often take the form of song24and typically come from a tune we already know. Researchers still cannot say why certain songs25in the mind more readily than others, and everyone seems to have a personal playlist of them. The likeliest candidates pair a simple, upbeat melody with repetitive lyrics that are26and easy to remember. Commercial jingles and slightly annoying radio27are prime examples. In addition, recent or repeated exposure to a song, or even to a small part of one, can set off an earworm, and so can word associations, such as overhearing a phrase that sounds like a line from a song.

While earworms might be annoying, they are not necessarily unwelcome. Many people who get them28finding the experience pleasant. Others feel29about the tune, neither delighted nor upset. Only a30of listeners, roughly one in three, are truly bothered by the music in their heads. passage.title: 久坐病的危害（The Dangers of Sitting Disease）
passage.text:
You've most likely heard the news by now: a lifestyle built around commuting by car, working at a desk, and watching TV can be harmful to our health. Researchers are increasingly21the long hours we spend rooted in our chairs to a host of health problems. In fact, the list includes so many22diseases that experts have named this modern-day health epidemic the “sitting disease.”

When we sit for hours on end, the body's metabolism23down. So does the rate at which enzymes break down our fat24. As a result, blood sugar levels and blood pressure both start to climb. If we stay seated, these numbers keep25upward, steadily damaging the inside of the arteries and driving up the risk of diabetes, heart disease, stroke, and other serious conditions. In essence, sitting too long brings about fundamental changes in our biology.

The good news is that small amounts of activity spread throughout the day, even just standing up and moving around, are enough to bring those levels back down. Better yet, such activity adds up, even when it comes in26of only two or three minutes. Thirty minutes of light movement broken up in this way can be just as27as a single half-hour block of exercise.

passage.title: 把海水變成飲用水（Turning Seawater into Drinking Water）
passage.text:
Most parts of Taiwan have access to sufficient fresh water for drinking. In many arid regions such as Saudi Arabia, however, water resources are limited, and fresh water can be in short21. As the world's population continues to grow, water shortages will occur more often, and the need for additional sources of water will become22. Some may ask, “Since the ocean covers more than 70 percent of the Earth, why not just get our drinking water from the sea?”

Turning seawater into fresh water requires removing the salt it contains, a process known as desalination. The trouble is that desalination23a huge amount of energy. Salt dissolves easily in water, forming strong chemical24that are difficult to break. Since both the energy and the technology involved are expensive, desalinated water can be costly.

Desalination carries environmental costs as well. Marine life can get sucked into desalination25and killed there. The loss of baby fish, plankton, and other tiny creatures throws the food chain off balance. Also, there is the question of what to do with the salt once it has been taken out. What remains is a highly26brine. Pumping this super-salty water back into the sea can27local aquatic life. Reducing these impacts is possible, but doing so adds to the costs.

passage.title: 海豚互叫名字（Dolphins Call Each Other by Name）
passage.text:
Imagine two bottlenose dolphins swimming in the Gulf of Mexico. From each of them comes a series of clicks, whistles, and whines, much like a21. We cannot be sure what the pair are discussing, but scientists do believe that dolphins call one another by “name.” A recent study suggests that each of these marine mammals produces its own unique22whistle. Moreover, a dolphin not only23the whistles of others it is close to and wants to see again but also mimics them. It seems that a dolphin can call a companion simply by copying that companion’s distinct sound. “They’re abstract names,” said Randall Wells, one of the researchers behind the study.

To24the study, the researchers listened to recordings, made around Florida’s Sarasota Bay from 1984 to 2009, of about 250 wild bottlenose dolphins. The study also included four25dolphins living at a nearby aquarium. Some of the wild dolphins were caught for a short time and held in individual nets, which allowed them to hear but not see one another.

The researchers found that dolphins familiar with each other would copy the whistle of a group member when the two were26by the nets. Most of this took place between mothers and calves or among males who were close27, suggesting that the behavior was friendly rather than hostile. This is somewhat like calling out the name of a child or friend who has gone28.

Whistle copying of this kind resembles vocal copying in human language, since for both, keeping social29strong appears to matter more than the immediate defense of resources. In this respect, dolphins differ from birds, which tend to call to one another in a more “aggressive context.”

If confirmed, the finding would mean that dolphins show a level of communication rarely found in nature. If dolphins can identify themselves and30their friends by name with just a few squeaks, it is easy to imagine what else they might be saying. However, as the study’s authors point out, all we can do for now is imagine.

We cannot be sure what the pair are discussing, but scientists do believe that dolphins call one another by “name.” A recent study suggests that each of these marine mammals produces its own unique22whistle. Moreover, a dolphin not only23the whistles of others it is close to and wants to see again but also mimics them. It seems that a dolphin can call a companion simply by copying that companion’s distinct sound. “They’re abstract names,” said Randall Wells, one of the researchers behind the study.

To24the study, the researchers listened to recordings, made around Florida’s Sarasota Bay from 1984 to 2009, of about 250 wild bottlenose dolphins. The study also included four25dolphins living at a nearby aquarium. Some of the wild dolphins were caught for a short time and held in individual nets, which allowed them to hear but not see one another.

The researchers found that dolphins familiar with each other would copy the whistle of a group member when the two were26by the nets. Most of this took place between mothers and calves or among males who were close27, suggesting that the behavior was friendly rather than hostile. This is somewhat like calling out the name of a child or friend who has gone28.

Whistle copying of this kind resembles vocal copying in human language, since for both, keeping social29strong appears to matter more than the immediate defense of resources. In this respect, dolphins differ from birds, which tend to call to one another in a more “aggressive context.”

If confirmed, the finding would mean that dolphins show a level of communication rarely found in nature. If dolphins can identify themselves and30their friends by name with just a few squeaks, it is easy to imagine what else they might be saying. However, as the study’s authors point out, all we can do for now is imagine.

passage.title: 小小免費圖書館（Little Free Library）
passage.text:
Todd Bol, a retired businessman, could never have imagined what would come of the wooden container he built on his deck one day in 2009. That small homemade project has since grown into a movement with truly global21.

Bol’s creation was a dollhouse-size structure that resembled a schoolhouse. He mounted the little house on a22and stood it on his lawn as a free community library in memory of his mother, a book lover and former schoolteacher. That humble prototype23the founding of Little Free Library (LFL).

LFL is a nonprofit organization that seeks to put small,24book exchange boxes in neighborhoods around the world. Its concept is simple: neighbors are invited to take a book, leave a book, or25one for another. Today, more than 50,000 of these libraries are registered in 70 countries.

Almost anyone can register with LFL and start a library, as long as the box is kept in good shape and26with books that are appropriate for the neighborhood. Because owners are free to design their own, the libraries usually look unlike one another, and the possibilities seem endless. One in California was built out of a used wine crate; another in Texas had tiny stairs and brightly colored walls. Once registered, each library is given a number on LFL’s website, where the LFL Index lists its location along with GPS coordinates and other information. Owners also receive a sign that27“Little Free Library.”

Passersby say they have become more28to pick up a book when they walk past one of these little libraries. Part of the appeal is simple29; the rest is convenience. Some sidewalk librarians add that they have met more neighbors since setting up a library in their front yard. Bol, too, is proud of the way Little Free Library is bringing communities together. “It’s started a neighborhood exchange. It gets people talking and more30with their neighbors,” he says. “This leads to them helping each other.”

records.explanation: post 學生先想到的是「貼文」或動詞「張貼、發文」，放進 mounted the little house on a ___ 讀不通，就轉去填 reach，以為 on a reach 是「放在伸手可及的地方」；可是表達這個意思要說 within reach，不說 on a reach。【作答線索】mount A on B 是「把 A 裝在 B 上」，on a ___ 要一個能把小屋架起來的實物。post 原本就是「柱子、樁」：籬笆的 fence post、路燈的 lamppost 都是這個意思。【文內驗證】前一句說這是玩具屋大小的小屋，同一句後半說它立在草坪上（stood it on his lawn）；小屋要立在草地上讓路人伸手拿書，底下就得有根柱子把它架高。

passage.title: 小小免費圖書館（Little Free Library）
passage.text:
Todd Bol, a retired businessman, could never have imagined what would come of the wooden container he built on his deck one day in 2009. That small homemade project has since grown into a movement with truly global21.

Bol’s creation was a dollhouse-size structure that resembled a schoolhouse. He mounted the little house on a22and stood it on his lawn as a free community library in memory of his mother, a book lover and former schoolteacher. That humble prototype23the founding of Little Free Library (LFL).

LFL is a nonprofit organization that seeks to put small,24book exchange boxes in neighborhoods around the world. Its concept is simple: neighbors are invited to take a book, leave a book, or25one for another. Today, more than 50,000 of these libraries are registered in 70 countries.

Almost anyone can register with LFL and start a library, as long as the box is kept in good shape and26with books that are appropriate for the neighborhood. Because owners are free to design their own, the libraries usually look unlike one another, and the possibilities seem endless. One in California was built out of a used wine crate; another in Texas had tiny stairs and brightly colored walls. Once registered, each library is given a number on LFL’s website, where the LFL Index lists its location along with GPS coordinates and other information. Owners also receive a sign that27“Little Free Library.”

Passersby say they have become more28to pick up a book when they walk past one of these little libraries. Part of the appeal is simple29; the rest is convenience. Some sidewalk librarians add that they have met more neighbors since setting up a library in their front yard. Bol, too, is proud of the way Little Free Library is bringing communities together. “It’s started a neighborhood exchange. It gets people talking and more30with their neighbors,” he says. “This leads to them helping each other.”

records.explanation: read 的主詞幾乎都是人，這一句的主詞卻是 a sign（牌子），牌子不會「讀」，很多人就覺得 reads 不可能，轉去填 post，想成「牌子上張貼著」。【句構線索】that 代替 a sign 當主詞，後面要動詞；主詞單數、講的是現在的狀態，要第三人稱單數現在式，選項裡合乎這個字形的只有 reads，post 的字形不對。【一字多義】read 用文字、標示、儀表當主詞時，意思是「上面寫著、顯示」：The sign reads “No Parking.”（牌子上寫著「禁止停車」）。英文把牌子看成「顯示出這幾個字」的東西，所以後面直接接文字，不需要介系詞。【文內驗證】空格後緊接著引號裡的 “Little Free Library.”，正是牌子上的字。

passage.title: 用燈光上網的 Li-Fi（Li-Fi: Wireless Data from Every Light）
passage.text:
Flickering lamps can bring on headaches. Yet if a light flickers millions of times a second—far faster than the brain can21or the eye can detect—that flicker might be harnessed to do something useful, such as transmitting data. That is the idea behind Li-Fi, short for Light Fidelity. The term was22by Harald Haas, a University of Edinburgh professor, in a 2011 TED Talk. There, he shared his23of “wireless data from every light.” Since then, Li-Fi has grown into a wireless technology that sends data at high speeds through light-emitting diodes (LEDs), an increasingly popular way to light up homes and public spaces.

Because it turns LED lights into networking devices, Li-Fi has several advantages over Wi-Fi (Wireless Fidelity). For one thing, it offers tighter24for local networks. Unlike the radio waves that Wi-Fi relies on, light cannot pass through walls or doors. As long as glass windows and other25surfaces are covered, only devices inside the room can connect to a Li-Fi channel, so hackers in remote locations are shut out. In addition, Li-Fi can operate in places sensitive to electromagnetic waves, such as aircraft cabins, hospitals, and nuclear power plants, because light does not interfere with radio signals. Li-Fi's biggest26over Wi-Fi, however, is speed: researchers have reached 224 gigabits per second in the lab, much faster than Wi-Fi broadband.

How might Li-Fi enrich everyday life? Wherever there is LED lighting, there is a chance to put Li-Fi to work. Streetlights fitted with Li-Fi could bring the internet to cell phones, making it safer to walk at night. The LED bulbs in traffic lights could keep drivers27on the weather and traffic conditions. Tourists could benefit as well, since local information would be easily28to visitors. At home, smart lighting could even offer parents a quick29for their children's internet addiction: switch off the lights, and their internet connection goes dark too.

passage.title: 從號誌臂到自駕車（From Signal Arms to Self-Driving Cars）
passage.text:
While waiting to cross a busy intersection, have you ever wondered who invented the traffic light? Most people credit John Peake Knight, an engineer from Nottingham, with this invention. As a railway manager in the 1860s, Knight specialized in designing signaling systems for Britain’s expanding rail network, and he saw no reason why the same approach could not be adapted to London’s crowded streets. Thus, he proposed a signal that borrowed the21arms used on railways: a horizontal arm ordered drivers to stop, whereas one lowered to a 45-degree angle told them to move on, much like a traffic director’s gestures. Red and green gas lamps were added for use at night, and a police officer was22beside the signal to operate it.

Knight’s signal, installed near London’s Westminster Bridge in December 1868, turned out to be23. Just a month later, a gas leak caused the lamps to explode, injuring the policeman operating the device. Deemed a public24, the project was dropped at once, and traffic lights were banned from British streets until 1929.

In the early 1900s,25of Britain’s traffic lights appeared in big American cities, where traffic was growing rapidly. Chicago favored systems with swinging arms, while San Francisco chose red and green lights instead. Across the country, inventors26patents for improvements on Knight’s ideas. A major breakthrough was the yellow light, invented by William Potts, a Detroit police officer. Installed in Detroit in 1920, Potts’ three-color system could27an added signal: “proceed with caution.”

Now, with the28of self-driving cars, researchers have begun to suggest that traffic signals are no longer necessary. In their view, cars approaching an intersection will automatically29their speed so that they can pass through while keeping a safe distance from other vehicles. In the near future, we may experience a form of traffic management that is truly30!

passage.text:
Thomas Moran, a famous painter in the 19th century, played an important role in the establishment of American national parks. His vivid paintings brought the21of extraordinary landscapes before the eyes of the American public, thus setting the stage for these regions to be widely recognized and formally established as national parks.

Moran came to the United States at age seven, when his family settled in Philadelphia. They had come from northwest England, the blackened heart of the Industrial Revolution: The main street of his hometown was “a dark, unattractive hole,” and the river running through it was a string of dirty water. That was all the nature the young Moran knew. By age 15, he had begun painting, with the landscape paintings of the British master J.M.W. Turner as his22. America, quite unlike the place he had left, offered him no shortage of scenery to paint.

Soon the23young painter was hired as an illustrator at Scribner’s Monthly. By age 34, he had been appointed its24illustrator. In 1871, he was asked to illustrate The Wonders of Yellowstone, a story by Nathaniel P. Langford, who had taken part in an expedition to Yellowstone. Langford’s25of its utterly fantastic sights made Moran eager to see this odd territory for himself.

That same year, Moran joined the first US government26of the Yellowstone region, traveling with the photographer William Henry Jackson. He spent two weeks there,27his sketchbook with the landscape’s most stunning sights. His watercolors—the first color renderings of the area—were presented to Congress along with Jackson’s photos and the team’s findings. These powerful images28the imagination of lawmakers. In March 1872, Congress made Yellowstone the world’s first national park.

passage.title: 把黃石畫進國會的畫家（The Painter Who Brought Yellowstone to Congress）
passage.text:
Thomas Moran, a famous painter in the 19th century, played an important role in the establishment of American national parks. His vivid paintings brought the21of extraordinary landscapes before the eyes of the American public, thus setting the stage for these regions to be widely recognized and formally established as national parks.

Moran came to the United States at age seven, when his family settled in Philadelphia. They had come from northwest England, the blackened heart of the Industrial Revolution: The main street of his hometown was “a dark, unattractive hole,” and the river running through it was a string of dirty water. That was all the nature the young Moran knew. By age 15, he had begun painting, with the landscape paintings of the British master J.M.W. Turner as his22. America, quite unlike the place he had left, offered him no shortage of scenery to paint.

Soon the23young painter was hired as an illustrator at Scribner’s Monthly. By age 34, he had been appointed its24illustrator. In 1871, he was asked to illustrate The Wonders of Yellowstone, a story by Nathaniel P. Langford, who had taken part in an expedition to Yellowstone. Langford’s25of its utterly fantastic sights made Moran eager to see this odd territory for himself.

That same year, Moran joined the first US government26of the Yellowstone region, traveling with the photographer William Henry Jackson. He spent two weeks there,27his sketchbook with the landscape’s most stunning sights. His watercolors—the first color renderings of the area—were presented to Congress along with Jackson’s photos and the team’s findings. These powerful images28the imagination of lawmakers. In March 1872, Congress made Yellowstone the world’s first national park.

passage.title: 胡佛水壩的誕生（The Making of Hoover Dam）
passage.text:
Located in Black Canyon, which straddles the border between Nevada and Arizona in the southwestern United States, Hoover Dam has been named one of the Top 10 Construction Achievements of the 20th century. Constructed between 1931 and 1936, it was the largest of its kind at the time. Building a structure so21was no small task. The effort involved thousands of workers and cost more than one hundred lives.

Since about 1900, Black Canyon and nearby Boulder Canyon had been22for their potential to support a dam that would control floods, provide irrigation water, and produce hydroelectric power. In 1928, the US Congress authorized the project, and the contract went to Six Companies, Inc., which had submitted the winning23.

However, no concrete structure of this size had ever been built before, and the builders had to rely partly on24techniques. The extreme summer heat and the lack of facilities near the site also25tremendous difficulties. Nevertheless, Six Companies turned the finished dam over to the federal government on March 1, 1936, more than two years ahead of26.

The dam’s initial design, which focused more on function than on appearance, was criticized by many as too plain and unremarkable for a project of such immense27. So Gordon B. Kaufmann, the architect brought in to redesign the exterior, greatly28the dam’s look and gave the entire project an elegant Art Deco style. An American illustrator, Allen Tupper True, was also hired to decorate the walls and floors of the new dam. He based his images and colors on Native American visions of rain, lightning, clouds, and animals. The patterns he created are29and appear both ancient and modern.

Today, Hoover Dam has become a national historic landmark. Standing more than 725 feet above the Colorado River, the highest concrete dam in the Western Hemisphere continues to30crowds 85 years after its creation, attracting more than a million visitors a year.

passage.title: 全黑隊的哈卡舞（The All Blacks’ Haka）
passage.text:
New Zealand’s national rugby team, the All Blacks, is widely credited with bringing the haka to the world stage. Just before kickoff, the whole squad will issue a warlike chant. Stamping their feet, slapping their thighs, rolling their eyes, and flicking their tongues, the players make21gestures in unison. This display, intended to heighten their morale and intimidate the opposing side, is a sight to behold. No other international sports team22a pregame ritual as powerful as the famed All Blacks haka.

What does the word “haka” mean? Many people regard it as an23term. In their minds, it covers all the Māori war dances traditionally used to frighten the enemy and prepare fighters for battle. Such dances, it is commonly believed, took place either on the battlefield just before combat or as the warriors were leaving their village on the way to a fight. In the Māori language, however, haka simply means “dance,” not “war dance.” Each dance comes with a chant that24feelings or tells ancient stories. While many haka are meant to be performed by men, others are open to anyone, male or female. There are even some haka that are25to women.

Thanks to the All Blacks, two haka have become widely renowned: Ka Mate and Kapa o Pango. The former was composed by a Māori chief in the early 1800s and recounts how he26his enemies. The All Blacks first performed it in 1906. The latter, a far more recent27, was written specifically for the team in 2005. The squad now uses the two interchangeably.

Today, haka of many kinds are performed at a wide range of ceremonial occasions, from the welcoming of28guests to birthdays, weddings, and the funerals of chiefs and others of high status. Though the practice was traditionally limited to Māori communities, it has since29far beyond them. Māori and New Zealanders of European heritage alike now take30in doing the haka, both on the rugby field and off it. The haka has become the most recognizable symbol of New Zealanders as a people.

passage.title: 全黑隊的哈卡舞（The All Blacks’ Haka）
passage.text:
New Zealand’s national rugby team, the All Blacks, is widely credited with bringing the haka to the world stage. Just before kickoff, the whole squad will issue a warlike chant. Stamping their feet, slapping their thighs, rolling their eyes, and flicking their tongues, the players make21gestures in unison. This display, intended to heighten their morale and intimidate the opposing side, is a sight to behold. No other international sports team22a pregame ritual as powerful as the famed All Blacks haka.

What does the word “haka” mean? Many people regard it as an23term. In their minds, it covers all the Māori war dances traditionally used to frighten the enemy and prepare fighters for battle. Such dances, it is commonly believed, took place either on the battlefield just before combat or as the warriors were leaving their village on the way to a fight. In the Māori language, however, haka simply means “dance,” not “war dance.” Each dance comes with a chant that24feelings or tells ancient stories. While many haka are meant to be performed by men, others are open to anyone, male or female. There are even some haka that are25to women.

Thanks to the All Blacks, two haka have become widely renowned: Ka Mate and Kapa o Pango. The former was composed by a Māori chief in the early 1800s and recounts how he26his enemies. The All Blacks first performed it in 1906. The latter, a far more recent27, was written specifically for the team in 2005. The squad now uses the two interchangeably.

Today, haka of many kinds are performed at a wide range of ceremonial occasions, from the welcoming of28guests to birthdays, weddings, and the funerals of chiefs and others of high status. Though the practice was traditionally limited to Māori communities, it has since29far beyond them. Māori and New Zealanders of European heritage alike now take30in doing the haka, both on the rugby field and off it. The haka has become the most recognizable symbol of New Zealanders as a people.

passage.title: 越來越小的大甲蟲（Big Beetles Getting Smaller）
passage.text:
Some of the world’s largest beetles are getting smaller because the places they live are heating up, according to new research from Canada’s University of British Columbia. Published in the Journal of Animal Ecology in January 2018, the study shows that climate change is having an21on these “teeny tiny” creatures.

The project began with a deep dive into the scientific literature. Evolutionary ecologist Michelle Tseng and her students combed through every article they could find, searching for laboratory studies on how temperature affects insects. Of the studies Tseng’s group turned up, nineteen showed that at least 22 beetle species shrank when researchers22them in warmer-than-normal conditions.

To see whether this pattern also held true for23populations, the team turned to the university’s collection of 600,000 insect specimens. Among them are thousands of bugs gathered locally since the late 1800s. From the eight species with the most24records, the researchers photographed more than 6,500 beetles. They also25climate data to track trends in rainfall and other factors besides temperature.

After sorting the beetles into size categories, the team found that five of the eight species had26in size over the past century. The four largest species, the snail-killer ground beetles among them, showed a 20 percent27in the last 45 years. Smaller beetles, in contrast, either stayed the same or even grew slightly larger.

Some ecologists are cautious about Tseng’s findings, pointing out that no one has yet proved rising temperatures to be the real cause of the shrinkage. British biologist Alan Ronan Baudron, however, is28. His own research has documented the shrinking of certain fish species due to climate warming. According to his29, warmer temperatures lower the concentration of oxygen in the water. As a result, fish burn energy faster and30at a smaller size. Even so, neither he nor Tseng believes that reduced oxygen, the cause he points to in fish, can also explain what is happening to the beetles.

passage.title: 尖叫的粗糙度（The Roughness of Screams）
passage.text:
Screaming is one of the primal responses that humans share with other animals. Conventional21holds that what sets a scream apart from other sounds is its loudness or its high pitch. Many sounds that are both loud and shrill, however, do not raise goose bumps the way a scream can.

To find out what makes human screams unique, neuroscientist Luc Arnal and his team examined a22of sounds containing sentences that 19 adults either spoke or screamed. The results showed that screams and screamed sentences shared a quality called “roughness,” which refers to how fast a sound changes in loudness. The loudness of ordinary speech changes only slowly, at rates between 4 and 5 Hz. In a scream, by contrast, the loudness can23back and forth far faster, at 30 to 150 Hz, so the sound strikes the ear as rough and unpleasant.

Arnal’s team then asked 20 volunteers to judge how24each scream sounded. Those rated the scariest almost always25with the highest levels of roughness. Next, the researchers used fMRI scanners to observe how the brain responds to roughness. As expected, hearing a scream boosted activity in the auditory centers, where incoming sound is processed. But activity also showed up in the amygdala, the brain’s fear center.

The amygdala is the area that26our emotional and physiological reactions to danger. As soon as a threat is27, adrenaline rises and the body gets ready to act. Screams, the study found, have a similar influence on the body. The researchers also found that roughness is absent from natural speech, whatever language is being spoken. Yet the same quality turns up again and again in28sounds. The most aggravating alarm clocks, car horns, and fire alarms all possess high degrees of roughness.

One potential29of this research might be to add roughness to alarms to make them more effective, the same way a bad smell is added to natural gas so that a leak is hard to miss. Electric cars, which are nearly30, could also be given warning sounds so that pedestrians can readily notice them.

passage.title: 牽引光束成真（A Tractor Beam Made Real）
passage.text:
In science fiction TV shows such as Star Trek, tractor beams are used to tow spaceships and move objects around. For years, scientists have labored to21such beams in the lab. In 2013, a team of British and Czech researchers led by Dr. Tomas Cizmar finally22the feat. They say they have created a real-life “tractor beam” like the one on Star Trek: a beam of light that can attract objects, at least at a23level.

Techniques for manipulating particles with light have been around since the 1970s, but this is24to be the first time a light beam has been used to pull objects toward its source. Ordinarily, when tiny particles are25by a beam of light, they are pushed along in the direction the light is traveling. After many years of research, Dr. Cizmar’s team discovered a technique that allows the radiation force of light to be reversed, so that the resulting negative force can draw certain particles toward the light source.

Dr. Cizmar says that even though the technology is still a few years away from practical use, it holds huge26for medical research. In particular, the tractor beam is highly27in the particles it can attract. Given a mixture, it can single out the ones that share certain28. The shared feature might be size, for instance, or composition. “Eventually, this could be used to separate white blood cells, for example,” Dr. Cizmar told BBC News.

Trapping objects such as spaceships in a beam of light has long been a classic plot device in science fiction films and TV series. But Dr. Cizmar said this particular technique would never lead to that. A29of energy takes place in the process. That is harmless for tiny particles, but it would be a serious problem for anything as big as a spaceship. Towing such an object would take a30amount of energy. The resulting heat could destroy it.

records.explanation: transfer 學生熟的是動詞「轉學、轉車」，看到 A ___ of energy 前面有冠詞，很多人沒想到它也能當名詞，就轉去填同樣是單數名詞的 potential，想成「能量的潛力」；可是 takes place 是「發生」，主詞要是一件事或一個過程，potential 是一種能力，不會「發生」。【句構線索】A ___ of energy 是「冠詞 + 名詞 + of + 名詞」，空格是這個主詞裡最主要的那個名詞，of energy 是修飾它的片語。transfer 的名詞和動詞同形，要看位置才分得出詞性。【作答線索】in the process 指用光束拉動物體的過程：光把能量傳給物體，物體吸收能量就會發熱，所以這一段接著說，能量轉移對微小的粒子無害，大型物體卻可能毀於產生的熱。
